tagline: Forest roads, a covered crossing and Roy Rogers’s farm country
intro: The Scioto Heritage Trail begins in downtown Portsmouth, meeting the Ohio River Scenic Byway near the city’s murals. Ohio’s byways brochure presents a route of forest land, canal remnants and the boyhood homes of Roy Rogers and Branch Rickey.

In Shawnee State Forest, the road network took shape during the 1930s, when seven Civilian Conservation Corps camps operated there. Four were segregated African American camps. Workers built most of the forest roads and five small lakes to supply the camps with water.

The journey starts at Portsmouth’s connection with the river byway. Friendship lies on U.S. Route 52; Shawnee State Forest occupies western Scioto and eastern Adams counties. At Otway, the covered bridge crosses Scioto Brush Creek, while Duck Run, near Lucasville, was home to the Slye family farm.

moments.title: Shawnee State Forest
moments.text: Shawnee’s woodland occupies land once worked for timber and building stone. From the mid-1800s into the early 1900s, quarried stone traveled by railroad to the Ohio River, then by barge; most went into Cincinnati buildings. The state established the forest in 1922 by purchasing 5,000 acres of cutover land. Now Ohio’s largest state forest, Shawnee includes both actively logged areas and approximately 8,000 acres of wilderness where roads and logging are prohibited. The forest surrounds Shawnee State Park and covers 63,747 acres of woodland in western Scioto and eastern Adams counties.

moments.title: Otway Covered Bridge
moments.text: The Smith Bridge Company of Toledo built Otway’s covered bridge in 1874. Its 127-foot timber truss crosses Scioto Brush Creek north of State Route 348. Bypassed and closed to traffic in 1961, it passed to the Otway Historical Society. Volunteers maintained the bridge, but it deteriorated; a tornado damaged its roof in March 2012. A federal grant followed that August, and repairs concluded with a ribbon-cutting in August 2014. The rehabilitation brought together the county engineer, historical society and engineering and construction firms, earning a state historic preservation award in 2015.

moments.title: Duck Run
moments.text: Before he became Roy Rogers, Leonard Slye learned horsemanship on his family’s Duck Run farm. The Slyes bought the farm in 1919 and built a six-room house. His father worked weekdays at a Portsmouth shoe factory because the farm could not support the family alone. With no radio, they made their own entertainment, inviting neighbors for Saturday square dances where Len sang, played mandolin and called the dances. He and his mother also used different yodels to communicate across the farm. Len attended high school in McDermott before his family returned to Cincinnati; Republic Pictures gave him the stage name Roy Rogers in 1938.
